topics.summary: Words that connect ideas across sentences: the former, anyway, mind you, in other words, namely, hence, thus, that said, let alone.
intro: **Cohesion** means making a text **hang together**: each sentence connects clearly to the next. We do this with **reference words** (*this, the former*), **discourse markers** in speech (*anyway, mind you*) and **linkers** in writing (*in other words, hence, that said*).

For basic linkers like *however* and *therefore*, see [And, But, Or, So, Because](/blog/grammar/and-but-or-so-because/#abo-however-therefore). For leaving words out and *do so*, see [Ellipsis and Substitution](/blog/grammar/ellipsis-substitution/).

points.title: This, such, the former and the latter
points.summary: Refer back to earlier ideas with ***this / that / these*** (+ noun), ***such*** (+ noun), ***the former*** (the first of two) and ***the latter*** (the second of two), so you don't repeat words.

rows: *He never says thank you. **This** really annoys me.*
*I'd never seen **such a** mess.* / *We need to avoid **such problems**.*
*I visited Rome and Paris. **The former** was hotter; **the latter** was more expensive.*

blocks.md: ***This*** + a **summary noun** (*this problem, this decision, this change*) is very common in good writing: it tells the reader exactly what you're referring to.
Use ***the former / the latter*** only when there are **two** things. For three or more, use *the first, the last*.

examples.text: Some people work from home. **This** saves them time and money.
The company cut 500 jobs. **This decision** was criticised.
Tea and coffee are both popular, but **the latter** has more caffeine.
**Such** behaviour is not acceptable.

mistakes.wrong: I like tea and coffee and juice, but the latter is my favourite.
mistakes.right: I like tea, coffee and juice, but the last is my favourite.

mistakes.wrong: I've never seen a such beautiful place.
mistakes.right: I've never seen such a beautiful place.

points.title: Anyway, by the way, actually, mind you
points.summary: Spoken **discourse markers** help you manage a conversation: ***anyway*** (back to the main topic / ending), ***by the way*** (a new topic), ***actually*** (a correction or surprise), ***mind you*** (BrE: adding a contrast), ***I mean*** (explaining), ***as I was saying*** (returning to a topic).

rows: return to the main point; finish
***By the way**, have you seen Sara?*
***As I was saying**, the plan is ready.*

blocks.md: ***Actually*** means *in fact*, not *now*: ***Actually**, I don't like coffee.* For *now*, use ***currently*** or ***at the moment***.

examples.text: **By the way**, your phone is ringing.
**Actually**, I've changed my mind.
**Anyway**, let's get back to work.
The hotel was old. **Mind you**, it was very cheap.

mistakes.wrong: Actually I'm working in a bank. (= now)
mistakes.right: Currently I'm working in a bank.

mistakes.wrong: By the way, as I was saying, the plan is ready.
mistakes.right: As I was saying, the plan is ready.
mistakes.why: returning to the topic: as I was saying

points.title: In other words, namely, to sum up, that is to say
points.summary: Signposting in writing: **order** (*firstly, to begin with, lastly*), **rephrasing** (*in other words, that is to say, i.e.*), **examples** (*for instance, e.g., namely*), **summing up** (*to sum up, in conclusion, overall*).

rows: ***To begin with**, the method is cheap.*
*in other words, that is to say, i.e.*
*The test was optional; **in other words**, you didn't have to do it.*
*for instance, for example, e.g., such as*
*Two students, **namely** Ali and Sara, got full marks.*
*to sum up, in conclusion, overall, all in all*
***To sum up**, the plan has more benefits than risks.*

blocks.md: ***Namely*** gives the **exact** items you mean; ***for instance / e.g.*** give **examples** from a larger group.
***i.e.*** = *that is* (it explains); ***e.g.*** = *for example*. Don't mix them up.

examples.text: **To begin with**, let's look at the costs.
He's economical with the truth; **in other words**, he lies.
Three cities, **namely** Paris, Rome and Madrid, were chosen.
**In conclusion**, both options have advantages.

mistakes.wrong: Many fruits, i.e. apples and bananas, are cheap. (examples)
mistakes.right: Many fruits, e.g. apples and bananas, are cheap.

mistakes.wrong: To summarise up, the results were positive.
mistakes.right: To sum up, the results were positive.

points.title: Hence, thus, consequently, accordingly
points.summary: Formal **result** linkers: ***consequently***, ***as a consequence***, ***thus***, ***hence***, ***accordingly***. ***Hence*** can be followed by just a **noun**: *He's from Rome, **hence** his name, Romano.*

rows: *The road was closed, **thus** causing long delays.*
*The town is built on a hill, **hence** the name Hilltown.*
*The data is old; **hence**, the results may not be accurate.*
*The rules have changed. Please act **accordingly**.* (= in a suitable way)

blocks.md: ***Thus*** + *-ing* shows a direct result: *Prices rose, **thus making** life harder for families.*
***Accordingly*** can mean *therefore* or *in a way that suits the situation*.

examples.text: The project ran out of money; **consequently**, it was cancelled.
She's a doctor, **hence** her interest in health.
The bridge was damaged, **thus** cutting off the village.
The guests are VIPs, so please treat them **accordingly**.

mistakes.wrong: The town is by the sea, hence it's called Seaside.
mistakes.right: The town is by the sea, hence its name, Seaside.

mistakes.wrong: Prices rose, thus made life harder.
mistakes.right: Prices rose, thus making life harder.

points.title: That said, admittedly, let alone, if anything
points.summary: Very advanced markers: **concession** (*admittedly, granted, that said, be that as it may, all the same*), **emphasis** (*indeed, if anything, not to mention, let alone*).

rows: ***Admittedly**, it's expensive, but it lasts for years.*
*The hotel was noisy. **That said**, the staff were lovely.*
*You may be right. **Be that as it may**, we can't change the plan now.*
*It was raining. **All the same**, we went out.*
*The task was difficult; **indeed**, it was almost impossible.*
the opposite, if there's any difference
*The new model isn't cheaper. **If anything**, it's more expensive.*
*I can't afford a bike, **let alone** a car.*

blocks.md: ***Let alone*** follows a **negative** idea and introduces something even **less** likely: *He can't boil an egg, **let alone** cook a meal.*

examples.text: **Granted**, the course is short, but it's very intensive.
The film was long. **Having said that**, I enjoyed it.
She doesn't speak French, **let alone** Russian.
The traffic wasn't better. **If anything**, it was worse.

mistakes.wrong: I can afford a car, let alone a bike.
mistakes.right: I can't afford a car, let alone a house.
mistakes.why: let alone: after a negative, something even less likely

mistakes.wrong: That saying, I still think we should try.
mistakes.right: That said, I still think we should try.

items.prompt: I don't have time to read a newspaper, ___ a novel.
___, the plan has some weaknesses. But overall, it's a good one.
The new manager isn't stricter than the old one. If ___, she's more relaxed. (one word)
items.explanation: *If anything* = the opposite is more true.

topics.summary: Ways to put emphasis on one part of a sentence: I do like it. It was Ali who called. What I need is a holiday.
intro: A **cleft sentence** splits one sentence into two parts to **focus** on the most important information: *Ali broke the window.* → ***It was Ali who** broke the window.* (not someone else) / ***What I need is** a holiday.*
We also use stressed ***do / does / did*** for emphasis: *I **do** like it!* See also [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/#sdn-formal).

points.title: Emphatic do: I do like it! Do sit down.
points.summary: Put ***do / does / did*** before the base verb in a **positive** sentence to add **emphasis** or **contrast**: *I **do** like your dress! She **did** call you. I don't eat meat, but I **do** eat fish.* ***Do*** + imperative is polite and warm: ***Do** come in!*

rows: *I don't drive, but I **do** have a licence.*

blocks.md: After ***do / does / did***, use the **base verb**: *She **does** work hard* (not *does works*). *He **did** tell me* (not *did told*).

examples.text: I **do** hope you can come.
He doesn't say much, but he **does** listen.
I **did** send the email. Check your spam folder.
**Do** have some more cake!

mistakes.wrong: She does works very hard.
mistakes.right: She does work very hard.

mistakes.wrong: I did told you about it!
mistakes.right: I did tell you about it!

points.title: It was Ali who…: it-clefts
points.summary: ***It is / It was*** + the focused part + ***who / that*** + the rest: ***It was Ali who** broke the window* (not someone else). ***It's the price that** worries me* (not the size).

rows: ***It was Ali who** broke the window.*
***It was in Paris that** I met her.*
***It was on Friday that** we left.*

blocks.md: Use ***who*** or ***that*** for people, ***that*** for things, places and times. Use ***It is*** for present and ***It was*** for past.
It-clefts are often used to **correct** someone: *No, it wasn't me who called. **It was** my brother.*

examples.text: **It was** my mother **who** taught me to cook.
**It's** the traffic **that** makes me late.
**It was** in 2019 **that** we moved to Canada.
**It wasn't** me **who** told her!

mistakes.wrong: It was Ali which broke the window.
mistakes.right: It was Ali who broke the window.

mistakes.wrong: Was in Paris that I met her.
mistakes.right: It was in Paris that I met her.

points.title: What I need is a holiday: what-clefts
points.summary: ***What*** + clause + ***is / was*** + the focused part: ***What I need is** a holiday. **What I like about her is** her honesty.* The focus comes **at the end**.

rows: ***What I love is** his sense of humour.*

blocks.md: The verb after *what…* is usually ***is*** (or ***was*** for the past), even when the focus is plural: ***What we need is** more teachers.*
You can reverse it: *A holiday **is what** I need.*

examples.text: **What** I really want **is** a cup of tea.
**What** worries me **is** the cost.
**What** I liked most **was** the food.
**What** you need to do **is** practise every day.

mistakes.wrong: The thing what I need is time.
mistakes.right: What I need is time. / The thing that I need is time.

mistakes.wrong: What I need it is a holiday.
mistakes.right: What I need is a holiday.

points.title: All I want is, the thing is, the reason why
points.summary: Other cleft patterns: ***All I want is…*** (= the only thing), ***The thing (that) I…is***, ***The reason (why)…is that***, ***The place where…***, ***The person who…***, ***The first / last / only thing…***.

rows: ***All I want is** a quiet life.* (= the only thing)
***The reason I'm late is that** the bus broke down.*
***The place where** we met **is** now a bank.*
***The person who** helped me **was** a stranger.*
***The only thing** I can do **is** wait.*

blocks.md: After ***The reason (why)…***, use ***is that*** (not *is because* in careful writing): ***The reason** I called **is that** I need help.*
After ***All*** and ***The only thing***, a verb focus can be a base verb: ***All I did was** ask a question.*

examples.text: **All I did was** ask a simple question!
**The thing I like most is** the food.
**The reason why** she left **is that** she was unhappy.
**The only thing** I can't eat **is** fish.

mistakes.wrong: All what I want is peace.
mistakes.right: All I want is peace. / All that I want is peace.

mistakes.wrong: The reason I'm late is because the bus was slow. (careful writing)
mistakes.right: The reason I'm late is that the bus was slow.

points.title: What she did was call the police; what happened was
points.summary: To focus on an **action**, use ***What*** + subject + ***do / did*** + ***is / was*** + (*to*) + base verb: ***What she did was (to) call** the police.* To focus on a whole event: ***What happened was (that)…***

rows: ***What she did was (to) call** the police.*
***What happened was (that)** the car broke down.*
***What I'm going to do is sell** the house.*

blocks.md: After ***What … did was***, use the **base verb** (with or without *to*): *What he did was **leave** / **to leave**.* Not *What he did was left*.

examples.text: **What** we **did was** take a taxi.
**What** you **need to do is** fill in this form.
**What happened was** that the bridge collapsed.
**What** I'm **going to do is** call him tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: What she did was called her lawyer.
mistakes.right: What she did was call her lawyer.

mistakes.wrong: What was happened was an accident.
mistakes.right: What happened was an accident.

points.title: It wasn't until, it's not that…it's that, that's what
points.summary: Advanced patterns: ***It wasn't until*** + time + ***that*** (= only then), ***It's not that … , it's (just) that…***, and **reversed** clefts: ***That's what** I mean. **This is where** the problem starts. **Here's why**…*

rows: ***It wasn't until** I moved abroad **that** I appreciated my family.*
***It's not that** I don't like you**; it's that** I'm busy.*
***That's why** I left. **That's exactly what** I meant.*
***It is** the customers **who** are affected most.*

blocks.md: ***It wasn't until*** can also start with ***Not until*** + inversion in very formal English: ***Not until** I moved abroad **did** I appreciate my family.* See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).

examples.text: **It wasn't until** midnight **that** they finally arrived.
**It's not that** the job is hard; **it's that** the hours are long.
**That's what** I've been trying to tell you!
**This is how** you open the file.

mistakes.wrong: It wasn't until I was 30 when I learned to drive.
mistakes.right: It wasn't until I was 30 that I learned to drive.

mistakes.wrong: It's not that I'm angry, but I'm tired.
mistakes.right: It's not that I'm angry; it's that I'm tired.

items.prompt: It wasn't until I read the letter ___ I understood what had happened.
I'm not angry. It's ___ I'm disappointed.
You need more practice. That's exactly ___ I said! (one word)

topics.summary: Avoiding repetition by leaving words out (ellipsis) or using short words like one, do so and so (substitution).
intro: Good English avoids **repeating** words. We can **leave words out** (*ellipsis*): *I wanted to go, but I couldn't (go).* Or we can **replace** them with a short word (*substitution*): *I don't like this shirt. Can I see a different **one**?*
For short answers and *so do I*, see [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/). For *I think so*, see the same page.

points.title: One and ones: the red one, these ones
points.summary: Use ***one*** (singular) and ***ones*** (plural) instead of repeating a **countable noun**: *I don't like this jacket. I prefer the black **one**. These shoes are nicer than the old **ones**.*

rows: *My phone is broken. I need a new **one**.*
*The **one** on the left is mine. The **ones** I bought were cheap.*

blocks.md: Don't use *one* for **uncountable** nouns: *I like white wine more than red* (not *red one*).
After *this / that*, *one* is often used: *I'll take **this one***. After *these / those*, *ones* is optional in BrE: *I prefer **those (ones)**.*

examples.text: This cup is dirty. Can I have a clean **one**?
The **ones** in the window are on sale.
I'd like a coffee. A large **one**, please.
**Which one** is your house?

mistakes.wrong: My bike is old. I want a new.
mistakes.right: My bike is old. I want a new one.

mistakes.wrong: I like green tea more than black one.
mistakes.right: I like green tea more than black.

points.title: I'd love to, I didn't want to: to instead of the whole verb
points.summary: Use ***to*** alone instead of repeating the **whole infinitive**: *Would you like to come? ~ I'd love **to**. I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.*

rows: *Would you like to dance? ~ I'd love to dance.*
*I meant to call you, but I forgot to call you.*
*You can stay if you want to stay.*
*He didn't go, although he promised to go.*

blocks.md: Keep ***to***: *I'd love **to**.* (not *I'd love.*) But after ***want*** and ***like*** in clauses with *if, when, what*, *to* is often left out: *Do what you **want**. Come whenever you **like**.*
With ***be*** and ***have***, keep them after *to*: *I'm not rich, and I don't want **to be**. I haven't finished, but I'd like **to have** by Friday.*

examples.text: Can you come tomorrow? ~ I'll try **to**.
I didn't want to leave, but I had **to**.
You don't have to help, but you can if you'd like **to**.
She isn't a doctor, but she'd like **to be**.

mistakes.wrong: Would you like to come? ~ Yes, I'd love.
mistakes.right: Would you like to come? ~ Yes, I'd love to.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't call her. I forgot it.
mistakes.right: I didn't call her. I forgot to.

points.title: She went out and bought milk: leaving out repeated words
points.summary: After ***and, but, or***, we often leave out a **repeated subject**, **auxiliary** or **verb**: *She went out and (she) bought some milk. I can sing but (I) can't dance. Ali ordered fish and Sara (ordered) chicken.*

rows: *He opened the door and he went in.*
*He opened the door and went in.*
*I've finished the report and I've sent it.*
*I've finished the report and sent it.*
*She plays tennis and she plays golf.*
*Ali drinks tea and Sara drinks coffee.*

blocks.md: You can only leave out words that are **the same** in both parts: *I'll call you and (I'll) explain.*
After a **comparison**, leave out the repeated verb: *She's taller than her brother (is).*

examples.text: We went to the beach and **swam** in the sea.
I've washed the dishes and **dried** them.
He can speak French but not **Spanish**.
My brother is older than **me**.

mistakes.wrong: She's tired and she's tired of her job. (repeated)
mistakes.right: She's tired of her job.

mistakes.wrong: I've cleaned the kitchen and I've cleaned the bathroom.
mistakes.right: I've cleaned the kitchen and the bathroom.

points.title: Do so, do that, if so, if not, I'm afraid so
points.summary: Substitute a whole verb phrase with ***do so*** (formal), ***do that / do it*** (informal). Replace a whole clause with ***so*** (*If so…, I'm afraid so*) or ***not*** (*If not…, I hope not*).

rows: *He was asked to leave, but he refused to **do so**.*
*I'll clean the car. ~ No, I'll **do it**.*
*Are you free? **If so**, come over. **If not**, call me.*
*Is it true? ~ I believe **so**. I told you **so**!*
*Will it rain? ~ I hope **not**. I'm afraid **not**.*

blocks.md: ***Do so*** replaces a verb + its object or complement: *Anyone who wants to leave early may **do so*** (= may leave early).
Use ***so*** and ***not*** after *think, hope, believe, suppose, expect, be afraid* and in *if so / if not*.

examples.text: Visitors may take photos, but they must not **do so** with flash.
Do you need help? **If so**, let me know.
Is the shop open? ~ I don't think **so**.
Have you finished? **If not**, keep working.

mistakes.wrong: She promised to call, but she didn't do.
mistakes.right: She promised to call, but she didn't do so.

mistakes.wrong: Is it going to rain? ~ I hope no.
mistakes.right: Is it going to rain? ~ I hope not.

points.title: Want a coffee? Sounds good. Seen Ali?
points.summary: In **informal speech**, we often leave out words at the **start** of a sentence (subjects and auxiliaries) when the meaning is clear: *(Do you) **Want** a coffee? (It) **Sounds** good. (Have you) **Seen** Ali? (I'm) **Sorry** I'm late.*

blocks.md: This is normal in **conversation**, text messages and emails to friends, but **not** in formal writing.

examples.text: **Looks** like rain.
**Got** a minute?
**See** you later!
**Anyone** want a sandwich?

mistakes.wrong: Dear Sir, Hope you are well. Want to apply for the job. (formal letter)
mistakes.right: Dear Sir, I hope you are well. I would like to apply for the job.

mistakes.wrong: Sounds like good.
mistakes.right: Sounds good.

points.title: As did we, than do most people, so would I
points.summary: Formal **comparative and additive** patterns use an auxiliary (often with **inversion**): *She was tired, **as were** we. They earn more **than do** most people. He loved the film, **as did** I.*

blocks.md: Inversion after ***as*** and ***than*** is **formal**; the normal order is also correct: *…than men **do**. …as I **did**.*
Make sure the **auxiliary** matches the tense of the first verb: *He **had** finished, as **had** I. She **will** win, as **will** you.*

examples.text: Ali left early, **as did** Sara.
City dwellers spend more on rent **than do** people in villages.
My parents were born in Iran, **as were** my grandparents.
He has passed, and **so have** I.

mistakes.wrong: She loves jazz, as does I.
mistakes.right: She loves jazz, as do I.
mistakes.why: auxiliary agrees with the subject: do I

mistakes.wrong: He had already left, as did I.
mistakes.right: He had already left, as had I.

items.prompt: The company's profits rose sharply, ___ its share price.
Older people tend to sleep less than ___ younger people.
My brother had already eaten, as ___ I. (one word)

topics.h1: Fronting and Word Order for Emphasis
topics.summary: Moving words to the start of a sentence for emphasis or style: On the hill stood a castle. Gone are the days when… Try as I might, …
intro: **Fronting** means moving a part of the sentence to the **start** to give it emphasis, create contrast or link it to what came before: *I can't accept **this**.* → ***This** I can't accept.*
Sometimes the subject and verb also change places (**inversion**): ***Gone are** the days when phones were just phones.* For the basics, see [Word Order](/blog/grammar/word-order/#wo-advanced).

points.title: On the hill stood a castle; off they went
points.summary: After a fronted **place or direction** phrase, verbs like *stand, lie, sit, come, go, run, live* can come **before a noun subject**: ***On the hill stood** an old castle. **Down came** the rain.* With a **pronoun** subject, there's no inversion: ***Off they went.***

rows: *An old castle stood on the hill.*
***On the hill stood** an old castle.*

blocks.md: This pattern is common in **stories** and **descriptions**. Use it with verbs of **position** or **movement**, not with *be* + adjective or verbs with an object.
With a pronoun subject, keep normal order: ***Here it is.** **Away she ran.** **In he came.***

examples.text: **At the end of the garden was** a small pond.
**Into the room walked** the president.
**Up went** the prices.
**Away they ran**, laughing.

mistakes.wrong: Off went they.
mistakes.right: Off they went.

mistakes.wrong: In the corner a piano stood old.
mistakes.right: In the corner stood an old piano.

points.title: This I can't accept: fronting objects and complements
points.summary: Put an **object** or **complement** first for **contrast** or emphasis, with **normal word order** after it: ***This** I can't accept. **The first film** I loved; **the second** I hated. **Strange people** they were.*

rows: *I liked the food, but I didn't like the service.*
***The food** I liked; **the service** I didn't.*

blocks.md: After a fronted object, there's **no inversion**: ***This** I understand* (not *This do I understand*).
Fronting is common when you **contrast** two things or **link** back to something just mentioned: *I've read most of his books. **His last one**, though, I didn't finish.*

examples.text: **Some** of the questions I could answer; **others** I couldn't.
**That** I really didn't expect.
**What he said next** I'll never forget.
**His name** I can't remember, but **his face** I know.

mistakes.wrong: This do I not believe.
mistakes.right: This I don't believe.

mistakes.wrong: The first part I understood it, but not the second.
mistakes.right: The first part I understood, but not the second.

points.title: Gone are the days, attached is my CV
points.summary: Fronted **participles** and **adjectives** + ***be*** + subject: ***Gone are** the days when… **Attached is** my CV. **Included** in the price **are** breakfast and dinner. **Lucky are** those who…*

rows: *The days when we wrote letters are gone.*
***Gone are** the days when we wrote letters.*
*Breakfast and dinner are included in the price.*
***Included** in the price **are** breakfast and dinner.*
*Those who have good friends are lucky.*
***Lucky are** those who have good friends.*

blocks.md: The verb ***be*** agrees with the **subject after it**: ***Attached are** my CV and references.* (plural) / ***Attached is** my CV.* (singular)
This is common in **formal emails**, **adverts** and **descriptions**.

examples.text: **Gone are** the days of cheap flights.
**Attached is** a copy of the invoice.
**Hidden** behind the trees **was** a small cottage.
**Included** in the package **are** flights and hotel.

mistakes.wrong: Attached are my CV.
mistakes.right: Attached is my CV.
mistakes.why: be agrees with the subject: singular

mistakes.wrong: Gone are the day when we were young.
mistakes.right: Gone are the days when we were young.

points.title: More important is, equally worrying was, such is
points.summary: Fronted **comparatives** and **evaluating adjectives** + ***be*** + subject: ***More important** than money **is** health. **Equally worrying was** the lack of staff. **Even more surprising** **is** the price.* Also ***Such is*** + noun + ***that***.

rows: *The lack of staff was equally worrying.*
***Equally worrying was** the lack of staff.*

blocks.md: This pattern links to the previous sentence and puts the **new, important information at the end**: *The hotel was dirty. **Worse still was** the food.*
The verb agrees with the **subject at the end**: ***Even more important are** the long-term effects.* (plural)

examples.text: **More worrying is** the rise in prices.
The film was long. **Worse still was** the ending.
**Of greater concern are** the side effects.
**Such is** her talent **that** she won at 15.

mistakes.wrong: More important is the facts.
mistakes.right: More important are the facts.

mistakes.wrong: Such the demand was that tickets sold out.
mistakes.right: Such was the demand that tickets sold out.

points.title: Try as I might, come what may, suffice it to say
points.summary: Fixed fronted patterns: ***Try as I might*** (= although I tried hard), ***Come what may*** (= whatever happens), ***Be it … or …*** (= whether it's), ***Suffice it to say*** (= I'll just say), ***So be it*** (= I accept it), ***Far be it from me to…***.

rows: ***Try as I might**, I couldn't open the jar.*
*Every job, **be it** big **or** small, is important.*
***Suffice it to say**, we won't go there again.*
***Far be it from me to** criticise, but…*
I don't want to… (but I will)

blocks.md: These are **fixed** expressions: learn them as they are. Most are formal, literary or ironic.
***Try as I might*** follows the pattern *verb + as + subject + modal*: ***Search as they did**, they couldn't find it.*

examples.text: **Try as she might**, she couldn't remember his name.
We'll finish this project, **come what may**.
All visitors, **be they** young **or** old, must buy a ticket.
**Far be it from me to** tell you what to do, but…

mistakes.wrong: Try as I tried, I couldn't sleep.
mistakes.right: Try as I might, I couldn't sleep.

mistakes.wrong: Suffice to say it, the trip was a disaster.
mistakes.right: Suffice it to say, the trip was a disaster.

items.prompt: The hotel was noisy. Worse still ___ the food.
More important than the price ___ the quality of the service.
Even more surprising ___ the fact that nobody complained. (one word)
___ as I might, I couldn't understand the instructions.
I'll be there for you, ___.
___ it to say, the meeting didn't go well. (one word)

topics.summary: Making claims more careful and less direct in academic and professional English: This may suggest… It would appear that… The results seem to show…
intro: **Hedging** means making a statement **less certain** or **less direct**, so you don't claim more than you can prove: *Coffee **causes** heart disease.* → *Coffee **may contribute** to heart disease.* **Distancing** shows the idea comes from **someone else**: *The minister **is said to** be resigning.*

Hedging is essential in academic writing, reports and polite business English. For *It is said that…* and *is thought to…*, see also [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

points.title: May, might, could, tend to, seem to
points.summary: Soften claims with **modal verbs** (*may, might, could*), ***tend to*** (= usually), and ***seem / appear to***: *This **may** be the reason. Young people **tend to** spend more online. The plan **seems to** work.*

blocks.md: ***Tend to*** + base verb describes a general tendency: *Men **tend to** be taller than women.*
***Be likely to*** + base verb = probably will: *It **is likely to** rain.* ***Be unlikely to*** = probably won't.

examples.text: Stress **may** cause sleep problems.
Older drivers **tend to** drive more slowly.
The new medicine **appears to** be effective.
Costs **are likely to** increase next year.

mistakes.wrong: Young people tend spend more time online.
mistakes.right: Young people tend to spend more time online.

mistakes.wrong: The results seem showing an improvement.
mistakes.right: The results seem to show an improvement.

points.title: Probably, possibly, largely, to some extent
points.summary: **Adverbs** and phrases soften or limit a claim: ***probably, possibly, perhaps, apparently, arguably, generally, largely, relatively, to some extent, in some cases***.

rows: ***Apparently**, the meeting has been cancelled.* (I heard this)
*She is **arguably** the best player in the world.* (you could say this)
***To some extent**, the plan was successful.*

blocks.md: Position: these adverbs usually go **before the main verb** or **after** *be*: *It **is probably** true. It **probably** works.*

examples.text: The decline is **largely** due to lower prices.
This is **arguably** the most important discovery of the century.
**To some extent**, the results support the theory.
**Apparently**, she's moving to Spain.

mistakes.wrong: The results are probable correct.
mistakes.right: The results are probably correct.

mistakes.wrong: In some extent, I agree.
mistakes.right: To some extent, I agree.

points.title: It would appear that, it could be argued that
points.summary: Impersonal ***it*** patterns make claims more **careful** and **objective**: ***It would appear that…, It seems likely that…, It could be argued that…, There is some evidence that…, This suggests that…***

rows: ***It would appear that** the data is incomplete.*
***It seems likely that** prices will rise.*
***It could be argued that** the law is unfair.*
***There is some evidence that** diet affects mood.*
***It is possible that** the results are wrong.*

blocks.md: ***Would*** makes *appear* and *seem* even more tentative: *It **would seem** that…* is more cautious than *It seems that…*
Use ***suggest*** (not *prove*) when evidence is not complete: *The results **suggest** that…*

examples.text: **It would appear that** there has been a mistake.
**It could be argued that** social media does more harm than good.
**There is little evidence that** the treatment works.
These findings **suggest that** more research is needed.

mistakes.wrong: It would appears that the plan failed.
mistakes.right: It would appear that the plan failed.

mistakes.wrong: It could argue that the plan is too expensive.
mistakes.right: It could be argued that the plan is too expensive.

points.title: Is said to have, would seem to suggest, reportedly
points.summary: **Distancing** shows that a claim comes from **others**, not from you: ***is said / thought / believed to (have)…***, ***reportedly, allegedly, supposedly***, ***according to***. Combine hedges for very careful claims: ***would seem to suggest***.

rows: *The company **is thought to** be in trouble.*
*He **is said to have** left the country.*
***According to** the report, crime has fallen.*
*The data **would seem to suggest** a link.*

blocks.md: ***Allegedly*** is used for **crimes** or wrongdoing that hasn't been proved: *He **allegedly** stole £1m.*
Don't combine ***according to*** with ***I*** or with opinion verbs: *According to the report…* (not *According to me…*; say *In my opinion…*).

examples.text: The painting **is believed to be** worth millions.
She **is said to have** written the letter herself.
The president **reportedly** refused to comment.
The findings **would seem to suggest** that diet plays a role.

mistakes.wrong: According to me, the plan is bad.
mistakes.right: In my opinion, the plan is bad.

mistakes.wrong: He is said to leave the country last week.
mistakes.right: He is said to have left the country last week.

items.prompt: The thief is believed ___ the country last night.
The CEO ___ resigned, although the company hasn't confirmed it.
___ to the latest figures, unemployment has fallen. (one word)

topics.summary: Using it as an empty subject or object: It's raining. It's easy to learn. I find it hard to believe.
intro: English sentences need a **subject**, so we often use ***it*** as an “empty” subject: ***It**'s raining. **It**'s five o'clock.* We also use ***it*** to **introduce** a long idea that comes later: ***It**'s important **to drink water**.* (= To drink water is important.)

This page goes from the basics to advanced patterns like *I find it hard to…* and *It goes without saying that…* For *It is said that…*, see [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

points.title: It's raining, it's 5 o'clock, it's 10 km
points.summary: Use ***it*** as the subject for **weather**, **time**, **dates**, **days** and **distance**: ***It**'s cold. **It**'s half past six. **It**'s Monday. **It**'s 3 km to the station.*

rows: ***It**'s 5 km from here to the beach.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: ***It**'s raining* (not *Is raining*).

examples.text: **It**'s very hot today.
**It**'s ten past nine.
**It**'s my birthday tomorrow.
How far is **it** to the airport?

mistakes.wrong: Is cold today.
mistakes.right: It's cold today.

mistakes.wrong: What time is?
mistakes.right: What time is it?

points.title: It is or there is?
points.summary: ***There is / are*** says that something **exists** or is in a place (first mention): ***There's** a problem.* ***It is*** describes or identifies something **already known**: ***It's** a big problem.*

blocks.md: Use ***there*** to **introduce** something new; then use ***it*** (or *they*) to talk about it: ***There's** a new film at the cinema. **It**'s really funny.*

examples.text: **There's** a bank on the corner. **It** opens at 9.
**There are** two bedrooms. **They**'re quite small.
Who's at the door? ~ **It**'s Ali.
**There's** no milk in the fridge.

mistakes.wrong: It's a supermarket near here. (first mention)
mistakes.right: There's a supermarket near here.

mistakes.wrong: There's very cold today.
mistakes.right: It's very cold today.

points.title: It's easy to learn, it's nice to meet you
points.summary: ***It's*** + **adjective** + ***to*** + verb: ***It's easy to** use. **It's nice to** meet you.* Add ***for*** + person: ***It's hard for me to** understand.* Also ***It takes*** + time + ***to***: ***It takes** an hour **to** get there.*

rows: ***It's difficult for children to** sit still.*
***It was kind of you to** help.*

blocks.md: This is more natural than starting with *to*: ***It's** easy **to** cook pasta* (not usually *To cook pasta is easy*).

examples.text: **It's** dangerous **to** swim here.
**It's** hard **for** me **to** wake up early.
**It was** nice **of** you **to** call.
**It takes** 20 minutes **to** walk to school.

mistakes.wrong: Is easy to learn English.
mistakes.right: It's easy to learn English.

mistakes.wrong: It's difficult to me to understand.
mistakes.right: It's difficult for me to understand.

points.title: It's a shame that, it seems that, it doesn't matter
points.summary: ***It*** + *be* + adjective / noun + ***that***-clause: ***It's a shame that** you can't come. **It's obvious that** he's lying.* With verbs: ***It seems / appears / turns out that…*** ***It doesn't matter whether / what…***

rows: ***It's a pity that** you missed the party.*
***It turned out that** she was right.*

blocks.md: ***That*** can often be left out in speech: ***It's a shame** you can't come.*

examples.text: **It's** a shame **that** the concert was cancelled.
**It seems that** the train is late again.
**It turned out that** we were in the wrong room.
**It doesn't matter** if you're late.

mistakes.wrong: Seems that we're lost.
mistakes.right: It seems that we're lost.

mistakes.wrong: It's a pity what you can't come.
mistakes.right: It's a pity that you can't come.

points.title: I find it hard to, I'd appreciate it if, make it clear
points.summary: ***It*** can also be a **preparatory object**: ***I find it hard to** believe. **I'd appreciate it if** you could help. **She made it clear that** she was unhappy. **I take it** you're not coming.*

rows: ***I'd appreciate it if** you didn't smoke here.*
***I hate it when** people are late.*
***I take it** you've heard the news.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: *I find **it** hard to sleep* (not *I find hard to sleep*). *I'd appreciate **it** if…* (not *I'd appreciate if…*).

examples.text: I **find it** easy **to** talk to her.
The teacher **made it clear that** phones weren't allowed.
**I'd appreciate it if** you could reply soon.
**I love it when** it snows.

mistakes.wrong: I find difficult to wake up early.
mistakes.right: I find it difficult to wake up early.

mistakes.wrong: I'd appreciate if you could call me.
mistakes.right: I'd appreciate it if you could call me.

points.title: It's no use, it's worth, it goes without saying
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***It's no use / no good*** + *-ing*, ***It's worth*** + *-ing*, ***It goes without saying that…***, ***It remains to be seen whether…***, ***It stands to reason that…***, ***It's not for me to…***

rows: ***It goes without saying that** safety comes first.*
***It remains to be seen whether** the plan will work.*
***It stands to reason that** prices will rise.*

blocks.md: After ***no use / no good / worth***, use ***-ing***: *It's no use **complaining*** (not *to complain*).

examples.text: **It's no use** arguing with him. He never listens.
**It's** really **worth seeing** the museum.
**It goes without saying that** you'll be paid.
**It remains to be seen whether** he'll accept the offer.

mistakes.wrong: It's no use cry about it.
mistakes.right: It's no use crying about it.

mistakes.wrong: It's worth to visit the castle.
mistakes.right: It's worth visiting the castle.

items.prompt: It's no use ___ to him. He won't change his mind.
It ___ without saying that we'll help you.
The museum is really interesting. It's worth ___ (visit).

topics.summary: Formal word order for emphasis: Never have I seen such a mess. Not only is it cheap, but it's also good.
intro: In formal or dramatic English, when a **negative or limiting word** starts the sentence (*never, rarely, not only, only when, under no circumstances*), we **invert** the subject and the auxiliary, like in a question: *I have **never** seen such a mess.* → ***Never have I** seen such a mess.*

If there's no auxiliary, add ***do / does / did***: *We rarely go out.* → ***Rarely do we** go out.* For inverted conditionals (*Had I known…*), see [Inverted Conditionals](/blog/grammar/inverted-conditionals/).

points.title: Never have I…, rarely do we…, little did I know
points.summary: After ***never, rarely, seldom, little*** at the start, use **auxiliary + subject**: ***Never have I** felt so happy. **Rarely do we** see snow here. **Little did she know** what would happen.*

rows: ***Little did I know** what would happen.*

blocks.md: The auxiliary comes **before** the subject, as in a question: *Never **have I**… / Rarely **do we**… / Seldom **does she**…*
With ***be***, invert *be* itself: ***Rarely is** the city so quiet.*

examples.text: **Never have I** eaten such delicious food.
**Rarely do** tourists visit this village.
**Seldom has** the team played so well.
**Little did we know** that our lives were about to change.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a beautiful view.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.

mistakes.wrong: Rarely we go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Rarely do we go to the cinema.

points.title: Not only … but also, not until, not once
points.summary: ***Not only*** + auxiliary + subject + ***but (also)***: ***Not only is** it cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.* ***Not until*** + time / clause, then inversion in the main clause: ***Not until** midnight **did** they arrive.* ***Not once*** + inversion.

rows: ***Not only is it** cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.*
***Not only does she** speak French, **but** she **also** speaks Spanish.*

blocks.md: With ***Not until***, the inversion is in the **main** clause, not in the *until* part: ***Not until** I got home **did I** realise* (not *Not until did I get home…*).

examples.text: **Not only did** he forget my birthday, **but** he **also** forgot our anniversary.
**Not until** the end of the film **did** I understand the story.
**Not once has** she been late.
**Not only is** this phone light, **but** it's **also** waterproof.

mistakes.wrong: Not only he forgot, but he also lied.
mistakes.right: Not only did he forget, but he also lied.

mistakes.wrong: Not until did I see the photos I believed it.
mistakes.right: Not until I saw the photos did I believe it.

points.title: Only when, only after, only then, only by
points.summary: ***Only*** + time / condition expression at the start, then **inversion** in the main clause: ***Only when** I got home **did I** realise… **Only after** the meeting **did** we know… **Only then did** she understand.*

rows: ***Only when** you leave home **do you** appreciate your parents.*
*I read the letter again. **Only then did I** understand.*
***Only if** you pay in advance **will you** get a discount.*
***Only in** Japan **have I** seen such clean streets.*

blocks.md: As with *not until*, the inversion comes in the **main** clause: *Only when I arrived **did I** see…* (not *Only when did I arrive…*).

examples.text: **Only when** it started to rain **did** we go inside.
**Only by** practising every day **can** you improve.
**Only then did** I realise my mistake.
**Only after** he left **did** I find his note.

mistakes.wrong: Only when I got home I realised.
mistakes.right: Only when I got home did I realise.

mistakes.wrong: Only by work hard can you succeed.
mistakes.right: Only by working hard can you succeed.

points.title: Under no circumstances, on no account, in no way
points.summary: Strong negative phrases at the start take **inversion**: ***Under no circumstances should** you open this door. **On no account must** you tell her. **At no time did** he say that. **Nowhere have I** seen…*

rows: ***Under no circumstances should** you leave the building.*
***On no account must** you touch the wires.*
***At no time was** the public in danger.*
***In no way is** this your fault.*
***Nowhere** else **will** you find such good coffee.*

blocks.md: These are common in **rules**, **warnings** and **official statements**.

examples.text: **Under no circumstances should** you share your password.
**On no account must** the children play near the river.
**At no time did** I promise you a pay rise.
**In no way does** this change our plans.

mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances you should open the box.
mistakes.right: Under no circumstances should you open the box.

mistakes.wrong: At no time I said that.
mistakes.right: At no time did I say that.

points.title: Hardly had I, no sooner, not a word did he say
points.summary: Very formal patterns: ***Hardly / Scarcely had*** + subject … ***when***, ***No sooner had*** + subject … ***than***, ***Not a (single)*** + noun + inversion (*Not a word did he say*), and ***So / Such*** + inversion (*So strong was the wind that…*).

rows: ***Hardly had** we sat down **when** the phone rang.*
***No sooner had** she arrived **than** she started complaining.*
***Not a single word did** he say.*
***So strong was** the wind **that** trees fell down.*
***Such was** the demand **that** the tickets sold out.*

blocks.md: Remember the pairs: ***hardly / scarcely … when*** and ***no sooner … than***. These patterns are mostly used in **writing** and storytelling.
Inversion is a **choice** for emphasis; the normal order is always correct: *We had hardly sat down when…*

examples.text: **Scarcely had** the film started **when** the power went off.
**No sooner had** I paid **than** I saw it cheaper online.
**Not a single person** **did** I recognise at the party.
**So loud was** the music **that** we couldn't talk.

mistakes.wrong: Hardly had I arrived than it started to rain.
mistakes.right: Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.

mistakes.wrong: Not a word he said. (formal inversion)
mistakes.right: Not a word did he say.

items.prompt: Hardly ___ the house when it started to snow.
___ was the storm that the airport closed.
Not a single question ___ she answer correctly. (one word)

topics.h1: Inverted Conditionals (Had I known…, Should you need…)
topics.summary: Formal conditionals without if: Had I known… Were she to leave… Should you need help…
intro: In formal English we can leave out *if* and put ***had, were*** or ***should*** before the subject: ***Had I known**, I would have called.* = *If I had known…*

These forms are common in formal writing, business emails and speeches. For the normal patterns, see [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

points.title: Had I known…: inverted third conditional
points.summary: **Had + subject + past participle** = *If + subject + had + past participle*: ***Had I known**, I would have helped.*

rows: *If I **had known**, I would have helped.*
***Had I known**, I would have helped.*
*If we **had left** earlier, we'd have caught it.*
***Had we left** earlier, we'd have caught it.*
*If she **had been** told, she'd have come.*
***Had she been** told, she'd have come.*

blocks.md: Drop *if* and put ***had*** before the subject. The rest of the sentence doesn't change.
It also works in mixed conditionals: ***Had I taken** that job, I would be living in Dubai now.*

examples.text: **Had** the weather **been** better, the event would have been a success.
**Had** they **listened** to the warnings, nobody would have been hurt.
**Had** I **studied** law, I would be a judge by now.

mistakes.wrong: Had I knew, I would have told you.
mistakes.right: Had I known, I would have told you.

mistakes.wrong: If had I known, I would have told you.
mistakes.right: Had I known, I would have told you.

mistakes.wrong: Did I know, I would have told you.
mistakes.right: Had I known, I would have told you.
mistakes.why: only had, were, should can invert

points.title: Were I…, Were she to…: inverted second conditional
points.summary: **Were + subject + noun / adjective** or **Were + subject + to + verb** = *If … were (to)*: ***Were I** in your position… **Were she to** resign…*

blocks.md: With *be*: drop *if* and put ***were*** first: *If I were in your position…* → ***Were I** in your position, I would accept.*
With other verbs, use ***were + subject + to + base verb***: *If the company moved…* → ***Were** the company **to** move, many jobs would be lost.*
Only *were* inverts. You can't say *Had I a car…* in modern English (it sounds very old-fashioned), and never *Did I have…* Use *If I had a car…* or *Were I to have…*

examples.text: **Were** I rich, I would start a charity.
**Were** the price **to** rise again, sales would fall.
**Were** you **to** accept the offer, when could you start?
**Were** she here, she would know what to do.

mistakes.wrong: Were I to was you, I would wait.
mistakes.right: Were I you, I would wait.

mistakes.wrong: Was I in your position, I would accept.
mistakes.right: Were I in your position, I would accept.

mistakes.wrong: Were he to lost his job, they couldn't pay the rent.
mistakes.right: Were he to lose his job, they couldn't pay the rent.

points.title: Should you need…: formal first conditional
points.summary: **Should + subject + base verb** = *If … happens (by chance)*: ***Should you need** help, please call us.*

blocks.md: ***Should*** + subject + base verb is a formal way to say *if* for a **possible but not very likely** future event: *If you need any help…* → ***Should you need** any help, please contact reception.*
It's very common in business emails, letters and notices. The main clause is often an imperative or *will*: ***Should** you **have** any questions, **do not hesitate** to contact me.*
The normal form with *if* also exists: ***If you should need** help…* (less formal than the inversion).

examples.text: **Should** you **require** further information, please let me know.
**Should** the flight **be** delayed, passengers will receive a meal voucher.
**Should** anyone **call**, tell them I'm in a meeting.
**If** you **should see** Ahmad, give him my regards.

mistakes.wrong: Should you will need help, call us.
mistakes.right: Should you need help, call us.

mistakes.wrong: Should you needed help, call us.
mistakes.right: Should you need help, call us.

mistakes.wrong: If should you need help, call us.
mistakes.right: Should you need help, call us.

points.title: Negative inversion: Had I not…, Were it not for…
points.summary: In the negative, put **not** after the subject: ***Had I not** seen it… **Were it not for**… **Should you not** wish…* No contractions.

blocks.md: For negative inverted conditionals, the word order is ***had / were / should + subject + not***: ***Had** I **not** seen the sign, I would have missed the turn.*
Don't use contractions: *Had I not…*, not *Hadn't I…* (which sounds like a question).

Two very common fixed phrases: ***Were it not for*** + noun (= if it weren't for) and ***Had it not been for*** + noun (= if it hadn't been for): ***Were it not for** your help, I would be lost. **Had it not been for** the rain, we would have won.*

examples.text: **Had** we **not** stopped, we would have hit the deer.
**Were it not for** the internet, I couldn't work from home.
**Had it not been for** her courage, many people would have died.
**Should** you **not** wish to receive our emails, click here.

mistakes.wrong: Hadn't I seen it, I would have missed it.
mistakes.right: Had I not seen it, I would have missed it.

mistakes.wrong: Were not it for you, I'd be lost.
mistakes.right: Were it not for you, I'd be lost.

points.title: When to use inverted conditionals
points.summary: Inversion is **formal**: use it in business writing, reports, speeches and literature. In everyday speech, *if* sounds more natural.

blocks.md: Inverted conditionals give a formal, careful tone. They're typical of:

items: business emails and letters: ***Should** you **have** any questions…*
notices, contracts and instructions: ***Should** the device **fail**, contact the supplier.*
reports, academic writing and speeches: ***Were** these measures **to be** introduced, costs would fall.*
storytelling and literature: ***Had** she **known** what lay ahead, she would never have gone.*

blocks.md: In conversation with friends, they can sound stiff: *If I'd known, I'd have called you* is the natural choice.
*Should you…* is the most common in modern English, especially in emails. *Were … to* and *Had …* are more typical of writing.

examples.text: **Should** you **wish** to discuss this further, I am available on Monday.
**Were** the policy **to be** extended, all employees would benefit.
**Had** he **turned** back then, the story would have ended differently.
If you'd told me, I'd have come.

mistakes.wrong: Hey, had you told me, I'd have come to the party! (to a friend)
mistakes.right: Hey, if you'd told me, I'd have come to the party!

items.prompt: Which sentence fits a formal business email?
options: Need more details? Just text me.
Should you require any further details, please contact me.
If you want more info, give me a shout.
Had you wanted details, you'd have asked.
items.explanation: *Should you require…* is a standard formal phrase.

items.prompt: You're chatting with a friend. Which sentence sounds most natural?
options: Had I known you were in town, I would have called you.
Were I to have known you were in town, I would have called.
If I'd known you were in town, I'd have called you.
Should I have known you were in town, I would call.
items.explanation: In casual speech, *if* is more natural.

items.prompt: Complete the formal notice: ___ (the lift / break) down, please use the stairs.

topics.summary: Turning verbs and adjectives into nouns for a formal, academic style: decide → decision, prices rose → the rise in prices.
intro: **Nominalisation** means using a **noun** where we could use a verb or an adjective: *They **decided** quickly.* → *Their **decision** was quick.* It makes writing more **formal** and helps you pack more information into a sentence.

Nominalisation is common in academic essays, reports and the news. But too much of it makes a text heavy, so use it with care. For other formal features, see [Hedging and Distancing](/blog/grammar/hedging-distancing/).

points.title: Decide → decision, important → importance
points.summary: Many **verbs** and **adjectives** have a related **noun**. Common endings: ***-tion / -sion*** (*decision*), ***-ment*** (*development*), ***-al*** (*arrival*), ***-ure*** (*failure*), ***-ance / -ence*** (*importance*), ***-ity*** (*ability*), ***-ness*** (*awareness*).

blocks.md: Some nouns are **irregular** and must be learned: *grow → **growth**, high → **height**, long → **length**, strong → **strength**, die → **death**, succeed → **success**, choose → **choice***.

examples.text: The **reduction** in costs was welcome.
We noticed a big **improvement** in his work.
The **arrival** of the train was delayed.
Nobody understood the **importance** of the meeting.

mistakes.wrong: The decide was made yesterday.
mistakes.right: The decision was made yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: There was a big grow in sales.
mistakes.right: There was a big growth in sales.

points.title: Because prices rose → because of the rise in prices
points.summary: In formal writing, a **clause** (subject + verb) often becomes a **noun phrase**: *Because prices **rose** sharply…* → *Because of **the sharp rise in prices**…* *When he **arrived**…* → ***On his arrival**…*

rows: *Because of / Due to **the sharp rise in prices**, …*
*The government decided to close the school.*
***The government's decision to close the school** …*
*They introduced new rules. This caused problems.*
***The introduction of new rules** caused problems.*

blocks.md: When you change the verb into a noun, an **adverb** often becomes an **adjective** (*rose sharply → a sharp rise*), and the **subject** becomes a possessive or an *of*-phrase (*the government decided → the government's decision / the decision of the government*).

examples.text: **The closure of the factory** led to many job losses.
**Failure to follow** the rules will result in a fine.
**On completion of** the course, you'll receive a certificate.
**The rapid growth of** the city has caused traffic problems.

mistakes.wrong: Due to prices rose, sales fell.
mistakes.right: Due to the rise in prices, sales fell.

mistakes.wrong: The quickly growth of the city surprised everyone.
mistakes.right: The rapid growth of the city surprised everyone.

points.title: Make a decision, carry out research, reach an agreement
points.summary: Formal English often uses a **general verb + noun** instead of a single verb: *decide → **make a decision**, investigate → **carry out an investigation**, agree → **reach an agreement***. Learn the right **verb + noun** partners.

blocks.md: These partners (collocations) are **fixed**: *carry out research* (not *make research*), *take action* (not *do action*).

examples.text: The police **carried out an investigation**.
After hours of talks, they **reached an agreement**.
The government must **take action** now.
She **gave a clear explanation** of the problem.

mistakes.wrong: We made a research on social media.
mistakes.right: We carried out research on social media.

mistakes.wrong: The team did a decision quickly.
mistakes.right: The team made a decision quickly.

points.title: Dense noun phrases, and when to avoid them
points.summary: Academic writing uses **dense noun phrases** with pre-modifiers (*a three-year government study*) and *of*-phrases. But **too many** nouns make a text hard to read: *There was an increase in the level of unemployment* is weaker than *Unemployment rose*.

rows: *There was a significant increase in the level of unemployment.*
*The implementation of the plan was carried out by the team.*
*A decision was made to conduct a review.*

blocks.md: Good academic writers **balance** nouns and verbs: use nominalisation to **summarise** or **refer back** (*This increase…*), and verbs to describe **actions** clearly.
**Pre-modifiers** pack information before the noun: *a study that lasted three years → **a three-year study***; *changes to government policy → **government policy changes***.

examples.text: The **three-year research project** was funded by the EU.
Prices fell. **This fall** surprised analysts.
Unemployment **rose sharply**.
**Recent government policy changes** have helped small businesses.

mistakes.wrong: We did an analysis of the data and a comparison of the results. (heavy)
mistakes.right: We analysed the data and compared the results.

mistakes.wrong: A three-years study was carried out.
mistakes.right: A three-year study was carried out.

items.prompt: Which is the clearest?
options: The team tested the new drug.
The testing of the new drug was carried out by the team.
The carrying out of the testing of the new drug was done by the team.
There was testing of the new drug by the team.

items.prompt: A study that lasted five years → a ___ study.
Sales rose by 20%. This ___ (rise) was unexpected. (one word)
items.explanation: Refer back with a noun: *This rise*.

topics.summary: Shorter, more formal clauses with -ing, past participles and having + past participle: Feeling tired, she went to bed. Built in 1900, the house is beautiful.
intro: A **participle clause** is a short clause with an ***-ing*** form (*walking*), a **past participle** (*built*) or ***having*** + past participle (*having finished*), and **no subject or conjunction**: ***Feeling tired**, she went to bed.* (= Because she felt tired…)
Participle clauses are common in **writing** and make sentences shorter and smoother. The most important rule: the clause must have the **same subject** as the main clause.

points.title: -ing clauses: at the same time, or because
points.summary: An ***-ing*** clause can show an action **at the same time** (*Walking home, I met Ali*) or a **reason** (*Feeling ill, she stayed in bed*). The subject is the same as in the main clause.

rows: ***Walking** home, I met an old friend.*
***Feeling** tired, she went to bed early.*
*She sat by the window, **reading** a book.*
***Not knowing** what to do, I called my dad.*

blocks.md: For the **negative**, put ***not*** before the *-ing*: ***Not having** a car, we took the bus.*
The clause can go **before** or **after** the main clause. Use a **comma** to separate them.

examples.text: **Hearing** a noise, he went downstairs.
**Being** a doctor, she knew what to do.
He left the room, **slamming** the door.
**Not wanting** to wake the baby, we spoke quietly.

mistakes.wrong: Not knew what to say, I stayed quiet.
mistakes.right: Not knowing what to say, I stayed quiet.

mistakes.wrong: Knowing not the answer, she guessed.
mistakes.right: Not knowing the answer, she guessed.

points.title: Past participle clauses: built in 1900
points.summary: A **past participle** clause has a **passive** meaning: ***Built** in 1900, the house is now a museum.* (= The house was built in 1900.) ***Written** in simple English, the book is easy to read.*

rows: ***Built** in 1900, the bridge is still in use.*
***Shocked** by the news, she couldn't speak.*
***Made** in Italy, these shoes are expensive.*
These shoes are made in Italy…
***Asked** about the plan, he said nothing.*

blocks.md: Compare: ***Seeing** the dog, the boy ran.* (the boy saw: active) / ***Seen** from the air, the city looks small.* (the city is seen: passive)

examples.text: **Painted** by Leonardo da Vinci, the Mona Lisa is very famous.
**Surprised** by the question, she didn't answer.
**Located** in the centre, the hotel is perfect for tourists.
**Given** the chance, I'd travel the world.

mistakes.wrong: Building in 1850, the church is very old.
mistakes.right: Built in 1850, the church is very old.

mistakes.wrong: Writing by a famous author, the book sold well.
mistakes.right: Written by a famous author, the book sold well.

points.title: The man sitting there, the car parked outside
points.summary: Participle clauses can replace **relative clauses**: *the man **sitting** there* (= who is sitting), *the car **parked** outside* (= which is parked), *people **living** in cities* (= who live).

rows: *The woman **who is talking** to Ali is my boss.*
*The woman **talking** to Ali is my boss.*
*The car **which was stolen** last week was found.*
*Goods **which are made** in China are cheap.*

blocks.md: Use ***-ing*** for an **active** meaning and the **past participle** for a **passive** meaning.
Don't use an *-ing* clause for a single finished action in the past: *The man **who broke** the window ran away* (not *The man breaking the window ran away*).

examples.text: Who's the girl **wearing** the red dress?
The houses **built** last year are already sold.
Anyone **needing** help should call this number.
The money **found** in the street was given to the police.

mistakes.wrong: The people waited for the bus were cold.
mistakes.right: The people waiting for the bus were cold.

mistakes.wrong: The book writing by her grandfather is in the library.
mistakes.right: The book written by her grandfather is in the library.

points.title: Having finished, having been told
points.summary: ***Having*** + **past participle** shows that one action happened **before** another: ***Having finished** my work, I went home.* Passive: ***Having been told** the news, she called her mother.*

rows: ***Having finished** lunch, we went for a walk.*
***Not having seen** the film, I can't comment.*
***Having been warned** about the storm, they stayed home.*

blocks.md: Use ***having*** + past participle when the first action is **finished** before the second, or to show a **reason** based on an earlier action.
With **conjunctions**: ***After finishing** / **After having finished** work, I went to the gym.*

examples.text: **Having lived** in Japan, she speaks Japanese well.
**Having been** invited, we had to go.
**Not having** studied, he failed the test.
**Having saved** enough money, they bought a house.

mistakes.wrong: Having finish the report, she sent it.
mistakes.right: Having finished the report, she sent it.

mistakes.wrong: Having been invite to the wedding, we bought a gift.
mistakes.right: Having been invited to the wedding, we bought a gift.

points.title: Dangling participles, and after / while / when + -ing
points.summary: The participle clause must have the **same subject** as the main clause. ***Walking** down the street, **the rain** started* is wrong (the rain wasn't walking). You can keep a conjunction: ***After leaving**, **while waiting**, **when using**, **once finished***.

rows: *Walking home, **I** got caught in the rain.* / *While I was walking home, the rain started.*
***While** I was driving to work, an accident happened.*

blocks.md: Conjunction + participle is common and clear: ***After finishing** the course, you'll get a certificate. **When using** this app, keep your phone charged. **Once opened**, keep in the fridge.*

examples.text: **While waiting** for the bus, I read a book.
**Before signing** the contract, read it carefully.
**Once opened**, the bottle should be kept cold.
**If stored** correctly, the medicine lasts for years.

mistakes.wrong: Arriving at the station, the train had left.
mistakes.right: Arriving at the station, we found that the train had left.

mistakes.wrong: Having eaten lunch, the bill was paid.
mistakes.right: Having eaten lunch, we paid the bill.

points.title: With prices rising, the work done, weather permitting
points.summary: **Absolute** clauses have their **own subject**: ***The work done**, we went home.* ***With*** + noun + participle: ***With prices rising**, people spend less.* Fixed expressions: ***weather permitting***, ***all things considered***, ***generally speaking***.

rows: ***The meeting over**, everyone left.* / ***The work done**, we relaxed.*
***weather permitting**, **all things considered**, **generally speaking**, **strictly speaking**, **judging by**, **considering**…*

blocks.md: Absolute clauses are formal or literary. ***With*** + noun + participle is common in both speech and writing.
Fixed expressions like ***judging by / from***, ***considering***, ***generally speaking*** are accepted even when the subjects are different: ***Judging by** his face, he's angry.*

examples.text: **The sun having set**, we lit a fire.
**With** the kids **asleep**, the house was quiet.
We'll have the party outside, **weather permitting**.
**All things considered**, it was a successful year.

mistakes.wrong: With prices rise, people are spending less.
mistakes.right: With prices rising, people are spending less.

mistakes.wrong: Weather permits, we'll eat outside.
mistakes.right: Weather permitting, we'll eat outside.

items.prompt: ___ so many people ill, the meeting was postponed.
We'll go hiking on Saturday, weather ___.
All things ___ (consider), I think we made the right choice.

topics.h1: The Subjunctive (I Insist That He Be…)
topics.summary: The base form after suggest, insist and essential that (that he see, that she be), were for unreal situations, and fixed expressions like if need be.
intro: The **subjunctive** is a special verb form. The most common type is the **base form** after verbs like *suggest, insist, recommend* and adjectives like *essential*: *I suggest **that he see** a doctor.* (not *sees*) *It's vital **that she be** on time.* (not *is*)

The subjunctive is **formal** and more common in **American English**. British English often uses ***should*** instead: *I suggest that he **should see** a doctor.* For suggest + *-ing*, see [Reporting Verbs](/blog/grammar/reporting-verbs/#rv-suggest).

points.title: Suggest that he see, insist that she be
points.summary: After ***suggest, recommend, insist, demand, request, propose, ask*** + ***that***, use the **base form** for every person: *They insisted **that he leave**. I recommend **that she be** careful.* British English also uses ***should*** + base form.

rows: past main verb: still base form

blocks.md: The base form doesn't change for *he / she / it* (**no -s**) and doesn't change for the **past**: *We **recommended** that she **take** the job.*
In informal British English, a normal tense is also heard (*I suggest that he sees…*), but in formal writing use the base form or *should*.

examples.text: I suggest **that you book** early.
The teacher insisted **that every student be** on time.
They recommended **that he take** a few days off.
The judge ordered **that the money be** returned.

mistakes.wrong: The doctor recommended that he takes a holiday. (formal)
mistakes.right: The doctor recommended that he take a holiday.

mistakes.wrong: She suggested me to see a doctor.
mistakes.right: She suggested that I see a doctor.

points.title: It's essential that he be…, it's vital that
points.summary: After ***essential, vital, important, crucial, imperative, necessary, advisable*** + ***that***, formal English uses the **subjunctive** (base form): ***It is essential that** every child **have** access to education.* Also after nouns like ***the suggestion / requirement / insistence that***.

rows: *It is essential / vital that* + base form
***It is vital that** he **be** told the truth.*
*It is important / crucial that* + base form
***It is imperative that** the work **be** finished today.*
***The requirement that** all visitors **sign** in is strict.*
*It is essential that he **should be** told.*

blocks.md: Compare: *It's important **to arrive** early* (general) / *It's important **that she arrive** early* (a specific person, formal).

examples.text: **It is essential that** the patient **rest** for a week.
**It is crucial that** nobody **find** out.
**It's important that** he **not be** late.
She ignored **the suggestion that** she **apply** for the job.

mistakes.wrong: It is vital that he is informed immediately. (formal)
mistakes.right: It is vital that he be informed immediately.

mistakes.wrong: It's essential that she arrives on time. (formal written)
mistakes.right: It's essential that she arrive on time.

points.title: That he not be told, that it be done
points.summary: The **negative** subjunctive is ***not*** + base form (no *do*): *I suggest that he **not go**.* The **passive** subjunctive is ***be*** + past participle: *They demanded that the law **be changed**.*

rows: *We asked that she **not tell** anyone.* (not *doesn't tell*)
*She requested that her name **not be published**.*

blocks.md: Don't use *don't / doesn't* in the subjunctive: *…that he **not leave*** (not *that he doesn't leave*).

examples.text: The doctor advised that he **not drive** for a week.
The report recommends that the factory **be closed**.
She asked that her address **not be** given to anyone.
We insist that the problem **be solved** immediately.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that he doesn't go alone. (formal)
mistakes.right: I suggest that he not go alone.

mistakes.wrong: They demanded that the rules are changed. (formal)
mistakes.right: They demanded that the rules be changed.

points.title: If I were you, I wish it were, as if he were
points.summary: The ***were*** subjunctive is used for **unreal** situations with **all** persons, especially after ***if, I wish, if only, as if / as though, suppose***: *If I **were** you… I wish he **were** here. He acts as if he **were** the boss.* In informal English, *was* is also common.

rows: *She talks as if she **were** an expert.*
***Were** it not for your help, we'd have failed.*
*If I **was** rich, I'd buy a house.*

blocks.md: ***If I were you*** is a fixed expression for advice: use ***were***, even in informal English.
For more on these patterns, see [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/).

examples.text: **If I were** you, I'd talk to her.
I wish my brother **were** here.
He behaves as if he **were** the manager.
**Were** it not for the rain, we'd go out.

mistakes.wrong: If I would be you, I'd go.
mistakes.right: If I were you, I'd go.

mistakes.wrong: I wish it is summer.
mistakes.right: I wish it were summer.

points.title: If need be, as it were, heaven forbid, long live
points.summary: Some **fixed expressions** keep old subjunctive forms: ***if need be*** (= if necessary), ***as it were*** (= so to speak), ***heaven forbid*** (= I hope it never happens), ***long live…***, ***God bless***, ***woe betide***, ***the powers that be***.

rows: *She's the boss of the family, **as it were**.*
***Heaven forbid** that anything should happen to him.*
***The powers that be** have decided to close the school.*

blocks.md: These are **fixed**: don't change the verb form (*if need be*, not *if need is*).

examples.text: We'll take a taxi, **if need be**.
He was, **as it were**, a second father to me.
**Heaven forbid** we should ever need it.
**Woe betide** anyone who forgets her birthday!

mistakes.wrong: I'll stay longer, if need is.
mistakes.right: I'll stay longer, if need be.

mistakes.wrong: Long lives the Queen!
mistakes.right: Long live the Queen!

items.prompt: We can borrow some money, if need ___.
___ anyone who touches my phone!
She became, as it ___, the voice of her generation. (one word)
